claims.text: The phase-transition onset and progression in heated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by temperature-activated selective surface dissolution.
Surface atoms with lower dissolution potentials are preferentially removed.
Atoms with lower surface energies preferentially leave or reorganize from the surface.
Selective surface dissolution produces a disordered, low-coordination outer layer.
Selective surface dissolution can produce an emerging core-shell configuration.
The altered surface layer triggers localized melting.
Surface-localized melting subsequently propagates inward through the nanoparticle.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid, crystalline, and elementally homogeneous.
The starting nanoparticles have uniform atomic coordination.
The controlled comparison restrains surface-atom motion in one set of simulations while allowing full surface relaxation and dissolution in another.
The comparison is performed near the nanoparticle premelting and melting regimes under a controlled atmosphere and without external catalysts or contaminants.
Differences in elemental surface energies drive surface rearrangement during heating.
Differences in atomic diffusion rates drive selective departure or rearrangement of surface atoms during heating.
Surface reorganization lowers the local melting threshold.
Element-specific surface depletion or reorganization should be detectable before or at the onset of melting.
Local melting should begin earlier at the surface than in the initially uniform solid baseline.
Restraining surface dissolution or surface-atom motion should delay or otherwise alter melting relative to the unrestricted condition.
The proposed mechanism is limited to the near-premelting and melting regime when catalyst effects and significant particle-shape variations are absent.
The exact melting-temperature shift and the contributions of individual elements are uncertain.

The hypothesis is falsified if no selective surface change is observed, constraining surface mobility causes no measurable melting-onset shift, or melting proceeds uniformly without detectable surface-driven effects.
